source: Numerics/Data/Time Series/TimeSeries.cs @ 2a0357a. Every value is curated with verify_oracles.py --dump against the real library; this file's job is the GUARANTEE rather than the accuracy, so it is asserted at ZERO tolerance throughout.
reference: The time-series layer's counterpart of fixtures/estimation/fit_cross_language.json, fixtures/toolbox/toolbox_cross_language.json, fixtures/callback/callback_cross_language.json and fixtures/ml/ml_cross_language.json: one case, three verbs, every assertion exact. Unlike the CALLBACK layer, whose limit is that a user's own R or Python arithmetic drives the run, everything here happens inside the shared C++ core -- the Mersenne Twister the two resamplers draw from, the kNN neighbour search under resample_knn (whose distance sort is the ported .NET introsort, so a tie resolves identically), and the calendar arithmetic under the clustering. So R-to-Python bit-identity is a real guarantee for this surface, not a best effort, and these assertions are what would catch it lapsing. The peaks-over-threshold block is deliberate: it asserts each event's DATE as well as its value, because a value-only assertion would pass even if a date conversion drifted, while the clustering itself depends on the calendar through the minimum-steps criterion.
